sentences.text: Giraffatitan brancai was a massive, four-legged herbivore belonging to the sauropod family, distinguished by an exceptionally long neck and tail.

Based on the nearly complete holotype — the specimen the species is based on — HMN SII housed in the Berlin Natural History Museum, the animal reached lengths of 21.8 to 23 meters and stood 13 meters tall.
Another specimen, HMN XV2, which possessed a fibula 13% larger than that of the holotype, is estimated to have been 23 to 26 meters long and weighed between 40 and 48 metric tons.
Despite its enormous body size, the creature had a small brain and skull, with a cranial vault volume of only 300 cm³.
From 1914 until the 1990s, this dinosaur was considered the largest known dinosaur and the largest land animal in history, a record that has since been surpassed by larger titanosaurians.
A mounted specimen at the Museum of Natural History in Berlin remains one of the largest and tallest skeletons in the world, a fact certified by the Guinness Book of World Records.

Most size estimates for the species rely on the Berlin museum mount, which combines authentic bones with reconstructions, and a frequently cited length of 22.46 meters was actually an addition error by the describer Werner Janensch; the correct length is 22.16 meters.
The discovery began in 1906 when mining engineer Bernhard Wilhelm Sattler found an enormous bone at Tendaguru near Lindi in German East Africa, now Tanzania.
The species G. brancai was originally described by Janensch in 1914 and named in honor of Wilhelm von Branca, who led the expedition that found the fossils in the Tendaguru Formation.
The genus Giraffatitan was established by Paul in 1988 and later elevated to full genus status by George Olshevsky in 1991.
Evidence from tooth wear patterns suggests Giraffatitan did not have a trunk, as the damage indicates biting and tearing plants rather than grinding pre-ripped vegetation.

Historically, scientists believed the nostrils were located on the top of the head, leading to theories that the animal used them like a snorkel to breathe while submerged to support its massive weight. However, studies indicate water pressure would have prevented effective underwater breathing and that its narrow feet were unsuited for aquatic locomotion. Research by Lawrence Witmer in 2001 suggests the nostrils were actually located near the snout tip, with the tall crests possibly supporting a fleshy resonating chamber.
A 2009 study estimated the Encephalization Quotient of Giraffatitan to be between 0.62 and 0.79, depending on the body size estimate used, reflecting its small brain relative to its massive frame.

Researchers have proposed that Giraffatitan may have possessed a proboscis to aid in feeding, though this hypothesis is disputed by some colleagues who note the facial nerve was not enlarged as in elephants.
The animal lived in meadows filled with ferns, bennettites, and horsetails, moving and feeding among vast forests of conifers, cycads, seed ferns, and ginkgos.
The type species of the genus Giraffatitan is G. brancai.
Giraffatitan fossils date to the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Tithonian stage, meaning the animal lived between 145 and 150 million years ago.
It lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic in what is now the Lindi Region of Tanzania.

It is debated whether the distinctive high-crested skull was a true characteristic of the genus Brachiosaurus, as the only known specimens of Brachiosaurus altithorax are now classified as Giraffatitan. While Daniel Chure rejected the separation in 2010, most studies have recognized Giraffatitan as a distinct genus since 2012.
